quotes.quote: Aider’s polyglot benchmark tests LLMs on 225 challenging Exercism coding exercises across C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, and Rust.
Aider excels with LLMs skilled at writing and _editing_ code, and uses benchmarks to evaluate an LLM’s ability to follow instructions and edit code successfully without human intervention.
By Paul Gauthier, last updated November 20, 2025.
OpenAI’s new o1 model with “high” reasoning effort gets the top score on the new aider polyglot leaderboard, significantly ahead of other top LLMs.

Contains coding problems in C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and Rust.
  The old benchmark was solely based on Python exercises.

Focuses on the _most difficult_ 225 exercises out of the 697 that
  Exercism provides for those languages.

Aider’s original code editing benchmark was
saturating as the top scores approached and then surpassed 80%.

The main goal for a new benchmark
was to re-calibrate the scale so that
today’s top coding LLMs
would occupy a wide range of scores between about 5% and 50%.

Models as old as GPT 3.5 Turbo were able to solve half of the
133 problems.

Exercism provides a total of 697 coding problems in those 6 languages.
A set of 7 of today’s top coding models each attempted all 697 of
the Exercism problems:

The new benchmark uses
the 225 problems that were solved by 3 or fewer models.
This achieves a balance between hard and moderate problems,
and provides a large but not excessive total pool of problems.

| Solutions found | Number of problems | Cumulative number of problems |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 66 | 66 |…| 7 | 258 | 697 |

OpenAI’s new o1 model established a very strong
top score of 62% on the new benchmark.
This still leaves 86 problems of headroom for future models
to solve.

The 225 coding problems are available in the
aider polyglot benchmark repo
on GitHub.

The “whole” format is the easiest for an LLM to use, but it uses a lot of tokens
and may limit how large a file can be edited.
Models which can use one of the diff formats are much more efficient,
using far fewer tokens.

Aider is configured to use the best edit format for the popular OpenAI and Anthropic models
and the other models recommended on the LLM page.
For lesser known models aider will default to using the “whole” editing format
since it is the easiest format for an LLM to use.

All pricing information is the cost to run the benchmark at the time it was
run.
Providers change their pricing and sometimes introduce entirely novel pricing structures.
Pricing is provided on a _best efforts_ basis, and may not always be current
or fully accurate.
This repository contains a curated collection of programming exercises extracted from Exercism's language tracks. These exercises are used for benchmarking and testing purposes.
All exercise content is copyright © [Exercism](https://exercism.org). These exercises are used in accordance with Exercism's open source licenses.

This
benchmark evaluates how effectively aider and LLMs can translate a
natural language coding request into executable code saved into
files that pass unit tests.

It provides an end-to-end evaluation of not just
the LLM's coding ability, but also its capacity to _edit existing code_
and _format those code edits_ so that aider can save the
edits to the local source files.

The benchmark is intended to be run _inside a docker container_.
This is because the benchmarking harness will be
taking code written by an LLM
and executing it without any human review or supervision!

# Run the benchmark:
./benchmark/benchmark.py a-helpful-name-for-this-run --model gpt-3.5-turbo --edit-format whole --threads 10 --exercises-dir polyglot-benchmark

The key statistics are the `pass_rate_#` entries, which report the
percent of the tasks which had all tests passing.
There will be multiple of these pass rate stats,
depending on the value of the `--tries` parameter.

You can see examples of the benchmark report yaml in the
aider leaderboard data files.
The benchmark is based on the Exercism coding exercises.

using os.path.exists() to verify a file’s presence before attempting to open it is a perfectly reasonable and common approach.
this mismatch between the test’s implicit requirement and the problem’s lack of explicit guidance leads to a failure in a one-shot attempt for this specific case

Hello. The same check as [#17](https://github.com/Aider-AI/polyglot-benchmark/issues/17) found five more JavaScript exercises (at `7e0611e7`) whose tests pass wrong solutions when run the way `benchmark/npm-test.sh` runs them.
Exercism has already fixed the first three, so syncing their current test files would close them.

**tournament** (12 tests). The example solution writes two spaces before the matches, wins, draws and losses. So any of those counts at 10 or more breaks its column: a team with 18 matches gets `| 18 |` instead of `| 18 |`.
No test reaches 10 in any of those counts, so it passes all 12. Exercism's current test file has the same 12 tests.

**rest-api** (9 tests). "add user" is only tested on an empty database. So a one-line change in `/add` passes all 9 tests: line 39, `user.name === payload.user` changed to `!==`, returns an existing user instead of adding the new one.

I found that the Go `counter` exercise can receive a passing grade with zero tests executed. In a frozen five-agent comparison using the Harbor Aider Polyglot adapter, the three completed agents currently show `go test` output containing `[no tests to run]` and receive reward 1.
This passing grade establishes successful compilation and an empty test invocation. Test-suite quality remains unmeasured for this exercise.
restores the declared test files before running the command and treats exit code 0 as success.
A human in a learning context would read the tests, then realise the need for the extra arguments, but from the information in the instructions and the scaffold alone, this is impossible to one-shot.
Every model I've tried has simply injected the 'answer' string in, then it fails the tests, then most of the time they can get it on the second pass.
I don't think whether it's 0 or 1 indexed, or whether there's a trailing newline is really a good 'software engineering' test.
I think having a trailing newline and it being 1 indexed is weird and if the models get that correct first go, it's probably data contamination.
